What a commercial landscape maintenance contract should actually cover
The scope gaps that turn a low bid into a stream of change orders, and the questions to ask before you sign.

The most common complaint property managers have about landscape contractors is not
that the work was bad. It is that the work they thought they had bought was never
in the contract to begin with.

A low bid wins because it is low. It stops being low around month three, when the
change orders start arriving for things everybody assumed were included. By the end
of the first year the cheaper contractor has cost more than the one that quoted
honestly, and the property has spent twelve months looking worse.

Here is what a maintenance scope should say plainly.

## Frequency, in writing, per service

"Regular maintenance" is not a frequency. Mowing, edging, weeding, hedge pruning
and irrigation inspection all run on different cycles, and each one should have its
own stated interval. If the contract says only that the contractor will "maintain
the grounds", you have no basis to say anything has been missed.

Watch for frequency that changes with the season. South Florida's growing season is
long, and a schedule that is right in February is wrong in July. A contractor who
has thought about this will say so; one who has not will simply visit less often
when the property needs them more.

## Who does the work

Ask directly whether the crews are the contractor's own. A great many are not. The
signs are consistent: an unmarked truck, crew in a different company's shirts, and
nobody on site who knows the property's history. Subcontracting is not automatically
a problem, but discovering it after signing always is — and it usually means the
company you vetted is not the company doing the work.

## What counts as an extra

Storm debris. Seasonal colour changes. Irrigation repairs. Plant replacement.
Palm frond removal. Each of these is legitimately quotable as an extra, and each is
routinely assumed to be included. Get the list of what is *not* covered, in writing,
before you sign. A contractor who is comfortable giving you that list is telling you
something about how they intend to invoice.

## Reporting

The single most valuable line in a maintenance contract is the one that says the
contractor will tell you about problems. A failing irrigation zone found during a
scheduled inspection is a repair. The same zone found after the turf dies is a
replanting. The difference is entirely whether somebody was looking, and whether
they told you.

## The question that sorts contractors quickly

Why South Florida commercial turf browns out — and which cause you actually have
Mowing height, chinch bugs, thatch and irrigation faults all produce brown patches. They need completely different responses.

Brown patches on a commercial lawn generate the same email every time: the board or
the tenant has noticed, and the property manager needs an answer. The difficulty is
that four completely different problems produce a nearly identical symptom, and
treating the wrong one costs a season.

## Mowing height

This is the most common cause and the easiest to miss, because nothing about it
looks like a mistake. St. Augustine — the dominant turf on South Florida commercial
properties — is cut too short far more often than it is cut too long. Scalping
removes the leaf area the plant photosynthesises with, stresses the root system, and
opens the canopy to weeds. The lawn browns, and the obvious conclusion is that it
needs water or chemicals, when what it needed was to be left half an inch longer.

A contractor running one mower height across every property in a county will produce
this on some of them. It is worth asking what height your turf is being cut at, and
why.

## Chinch bugs

Chinch bug pressure in South Florida is effectively year-round, and St. Augustine is
their preferred host. The damage pattern is characteristic: irregular patches in the
sunniest, driest part of the lawn — often along pavements and parking edges where
heat is reflected — that expand outward and do not recover with watering.

The test is simple and worth doing before anybody applies anything. Push apart the
turf at the edge of a browning patch, in the green tissue rather than the dead
centre, and look for small dark insects moving at the soil line.

## Thatch

Thatch builds fast in a long growing season. Past about half an inch it starts
behaving like a sponge that holds water at the surface and keeps it from the roots,
so the lawn is simultaneously overwatered and drought-stressed. It also makes
insecticide and fertiliser applications far less effective, which is why a property
with a thatch problem often appears not to respond to treatment.

## Irrigation

The one that is most often blamed on the landscaper and least often caused by them.
A broken head, an arc rotated to point at a pavement, or a zone that has silently
stopped running produces dry patches with hard geometric edges — a straight line or
a fan shape, rather than the irregular spread of a pest problem.

This is the strongest argument for inspecting irrigation on a schedule instead of
after a complaint. The pattern of the brown patch tells you which problem you have,
and a contractor who checks coverage first will not spend your budget treating for
insects that were never there.

## The order to work through it

Look at the shape of the patch. Geometric edges point at irrigation. Irregular
spread in the hottest part of the lawn points at chinch bugs. Uniform thinning
across the whole property points at mowing height or thatch.

Diagnose, then treat. That is the entire principle behind Integrated Pest
Management, and it is the difference between fixing a lawn and spending a summer
applying things to it.

Why your hedges look bad a month after they are cut
Shearing and pruning are not the same operation, and on a commercial property the difference shows up within weeks.

A hedge is cut, it looks sharp for a fortnight, and then it does not. The outer
surface goes shaggy, the base thins out, and by the next scheduled visit the whole
thing needs doing again. This is usually not neglect. It is the predictable result
of shearing a plant that needed pruning.

## What shearing actually does

Shearing cuts everything at a uniform plane, regardless of where the cut falls on
each stem. It is fast, it looks immediately tidy, and it triggers a specific
response from the plant: dense new shoots at every cut tip.

That dense outer shell is the problem. It shades the interior, the inner foliage
dies back, and the hedge becomes a thin green skin over bare wood. Once that has
happened, the plant cannot be cut back into the bare interior without leaving a hole
that may take a season or more to fill — so each cut has to stay slightly outside
the last one, and the hedge slowly grows out of its allotted space year after year.

## What pruning does instead

Pruning cuts to the plant's structure: back to a lateral branch or an outward-facing
bud, so growth is directed rather than simply stimulated. It takes longer, it looks
less immediately geometric on the day, and it holds its shape considerably longer.
More importantly, it keeps light reaching the interior, so the plant retains foliage
through its depth and can be cut back when it eventually needs to be.

On a commercial property, this is a budget question as much as a horticultural one.
Shearing needs doing more often, degrades the plant material, and eventually forces
a hard renovation cut or a replacement planting that nobody budgeted for.

## What to look for on your own property

Push a hand into the hedge past the outer surface. If you find bare woody stems
within a few inches, it is being sheared. If you find foliage most of the way in, it
is being pruned.

Then look at the shape. A hedge maintained correctly is very slightly wider at the
base than at the top, so the lower foliage still receives light. A hedge that is
vertical-sided or wider at the top is guaranteed to thin out at the bottom — and the
bottom is the part at eye level for everyone walking past it.

## Why cycle matters more than technique

Even correct pruning fails if it happens on complaint rather than on schedule. South
Florida's growing season gives a hedge a great deal of time to get away from you, and
a plant allowed to overgrow can generally only be brought back with the kind of hard
cut that leaves it looking damaged for months.

The cheapest hedge on a property is the one that has never been allowed to get out
of shape.

What pruning does instead

Pruning cuts to the plant’s structure: back to a lateral branch or an outward-facing bud, so growth is directed rather than simply stimulated. It takes longer, it looks less immediately geometric on the day, and it holds its shape considerably longer. More importantly, it keeps light reaching the interior, so the plant retains foliage through its depth and can be cut back when it eventually needs to be.

On a commercial property, this is a budget question as much as a horticultural one. Shearing needs doing more often, degrades the plant material, and eventually forces a hard renovation cut or a replacement planting that nobody budgeted for.

What to look for on your own property

Push a hand into the hedge past the outer surface. If you find bare woody stems within a few inches, it is being sheared. If you find foliage most of the way in, it is being pruned.

Then look at the shape. A hedge maintained correctly is very slightly wider at the base than at the top, so the lower foliage still receives light. A hedge that is vertical-sided or wider at the top is guaranteed to thin out at the bottom — and the bottom is the part at eye level for everyone walking past it.

Why cycle matters more than technique

Even correct pruning fails if it happens on complaint rather than on schedule. South Florida’s growing season gives a hedge a great deal of time to get away from you, and a plant allowed to overgrow can generally only be brought back with the kind of hard cut that leaves it looking damaged for months.

The cheapest hedge on a property is the one that has never been allowed to get out of shape.
